note: Each claim is tagged. 'sourced' claims paraphrase the cited page. 'general_consideration' claims are standard engineering prompts for investigation, not findings from a source, and must be presented as hypotheses.

measures.name: Raise the roadway profile (raised roadway barrier)
measures.summary: Raise the road (and usually sidewalks) so the road itself acts as a flood barrier and/or stays above design flood elevation.

claims.text: The guideline sample considers raised roadways with a 4-ft grade change, and notes the approach may also apply to elevating emergency evacuation routes.
Option 1 (retaining walls and/or slopes) may be feasible where buildings are set back at least 14 ft from the back of sidewalk.
The guidelines do not recommend a raised roadway barrier where existing buildings sit at the back of sidewalk; raising only the roadway creates safety, drainage, ADA and access impacts.
Once a street is raised, a stormwater pump system (pumps, generators) adds ongoing O&M cost; the guideline expects stormwater costs to be significant, citing Miami Beach raised-road projects.
Raising one corridor does not by itself block flood pathways that enter around its ends or through adjacent low ground.

exclude_if.reason: Guideline does not recommend raised roadway where buildings are within ~14 ft of back of sidewalk (S11.sec6 p.51).

failure_modes: Flanking around the ends of the raised section
Ponding behind the raised road without pumped drainage
required_data: Surveyed road and adjacent grade elevations with vertical datum

measures.name: Vegetated berm / landscaped embankment along the flood side
measures.summary: An earthen, planted embankment with crest and access paths placed between the water and the road.

claims.text: The guideline sample berm extends about 2,000 ft with an assumed grade change of about 2 ft for 2030 design flood elevation (DFE) conditions, with an incremental 2070 raise considered.
The sample design drawings tabulate crest, slope, and access-path widths by height, so a berm needs a horizontal footprint that grows with height.
The Morrissey study's key findings say coastal resilience measures should focus on nature-based solutions.
A berm only protects the road if it ties into high ground at both ends; otherwise water can route around it.

failure_modes: Seepage through or under the embankment
required_data: Available open space and ownership on the flood side
Topography (LiDAR is a start, survey needed)

measures.name: Raise / extend an existing seawall or waterfront edge
measures.summary: Add height to an existing waterfront wall and raise grades behind it.

claims.text: The guideline sample adds a 4-ft extension to an existing stone masonry seawall, raises grades about 2 ft behind it, and considers a deployable handrail barrier for later increases.
The guideline states the sample Harborwalk barrier alone would not address flood pathways in the area.
Costs assume the existing seawall can be extended without foundation modifications; a geotechnical investigation is required and may change costs significantly.

failure_modes: Existing wall foundation cannot carry added height
Flood pathways bypass the wall segment
Overtopping during events above design level
required_data: Survey within ~100 ft of alignment incl. utilities and resources (per S11.sec5 recommended studies)

measures.name: Deployable (temporary) flood barrier
measures.summary: Barriers deployed before or during a flood and retracted afterward; may be an interim measure.

claims.text: The guideline defines deployable barriers as systems deployed before and/or during a flood event and retracted afterward, and lists types from pre-installed and passive systems to mobile units and water-filled tubes.
The guideline presents a comparison matrix rather than a sample site; product mentions are not endorsements.
Deployment depends on forecast lead time, trained crews, storage, and access; a barrier placed across a road closes that road while deployed.

failure_modes: Seepage at joints or under the base
Blocks the road it is meant to protect while deployed
required_data: Warning time available for the relevant flood type

measures.name: Drainage, backflow prevention, and stormwater storage
measures.summary: Address water that enters through or ponds on the road via the drainage system (tide gates/check valves, inlet capacity, storage, pumping).

claims.text: The Morrissey study notes stormwater flooding may be a significant problem in the Central section because there is limited gravity to discharge stormwater at high tide.
The Morrissey study evaluated tide-gate options (including No Tide Gate and Hybrid) combined with raising the basin-side beach/dune/berm and a bay-side barrier.
Drainage works alone do not stop coastal surge from overtopping a road; they address rainfall and backflow pathways.

failure_modes: Mismatch between rainfall and surge drivers
required_data: Rainfall vs surge contribution to the documented flooding

measures.name: Strengthen alternate access routes
measures.summary: Rather than protecting this corridor, investigate whether improving a detour route preserves the same journeys.

claims.text: Whether a detour exists, and how long it is, comes from the network analysis for this corridor (see network impact).
A detour is only useful if it is itself outside the flood scenario footprint and has capacity for diverted traffic.

failure_modes: Detour floods in the same scenario
Detour lacks capacity or emergency-vehicle suitability
required_data: Flood exposure of the detour roads
